This report is unedited. Discrepancies may occur for which the Ontario Geological Survey does 
not assume liability. Recommendations and statements of opinion expressed are those of the author or 
authors and are not to be construed as statements of government policy.

al or Resident Geologist's office as to whether there is a copy of this report that may be borrowed.

rangements. A copy of this report is available for Inter-Library Loan.

### page_7
ONTARIO GEOSCIENCE RESEARCH GRANT PROGRAM
Final Research Reports, 1983
Preface
This publication includes one final report on a research project 
that terminated March 31 f 1981 and was funded under the Ontario 
Geoscience Research Grant Program. A requirement of the Program 
is that recipients of grants are to submit final reports within 
six months after termination of funding.
A final report is defined as a comprehensive summary stating the 
findings obtained during the tenure of the grant, together with 
supporting data. It may consist, in part, of reprints or preprints 
of publications and copies of addresses given at scientific meetings.
It is not the intent of the Ontario Geological Survey to formally 
publish the final reports for wide distribution but rather to en 
courage the recipients of grants to seek publication in appropriate 
scientific journals whenever possible. The Survey, however, also 
has an obligation to ensure that the results of the research are 
made available to the public at an early date. Although final 
reports are the property of the applicants and the sponsoring agencies, 
they may also be placed on an open file. This report is intended to 
meet this obligation.
E.G. Pye 
Director 
Ontario Geological Survey

### page_12
I. COMPONENT MAGNETIZATION OF ALGOMAN BANDED FORMATIONS
AND DEPOSITS IN ONTARIO
D. T. A. Symons and M. Stupavsky
Department of Geology, University of Windsor
Windsor, Ontario, N9B 3P4

### page_13
INTRODUCTION
This study was performed as four related but separate studies of 
Algoman-type banded iron formations (BIF) in Ontario. The results of the 
study for the Sherman Mine near Temagami have been reported in full by 
Symons and Stupavsky (1979,1980), for the Moose Mountain Mine near Capreol 
by Symons et al (1980), for the Adams Mine near Kirkland Lake by Symons 
et al (1981), and for the Griffiths Mine near Red Lake by Symons et al 
(1982). The latter study forms the second article in this Open File 
Report. The purpose of this article is to summarize the results of the 
four studies primarily in tabular form with relevant comments. Details 
concerning the geology, sampling methods and locations, experimental and 
statistical methods, and detailed interpretations are given© in the original 
references.
GEOLOGICAL FEATURES
All of the four iron formation deposits are Archean BIF of the 
magnetite oxide facies with three located in the Abitibi Belt and one in 
the Uchi Belt of the Superior Province in the Canadian Shield. The BIF 
horizons range in thickness from -50 to -150 m and are interlayered with 
siliceous metasediments associated with Archean metavolcanics of basic to 
acidic composition. These strata were deformed during the Kenoran Orogeny 
at -2.55 Ga at which time minor basic and large acidic plutons were 
emplaced adjacent to or within a few kilometers of the deposits. All 
were isoclinally deformed to produce intermediate to steeply dipping limbs.

### page_15
Repetition of the BIF member in adjacent faulted segments or in synclinal 
structures provided more economic thicknesses of ore at the Adams and 
Griffiths Mines. Subsequently minor relatively undeformed late dikes of 
generally basic composition were intruded into the Archean rocks. In the 
Abitibi Belt, these rocks are unconformably overlain by Huronian strata 
of -2.3 Ga age. All of the BIF have been regionally metamorphosed to the 
lower to middle greenschist facies, however, significant portions of all 
except the Sherman Mine have been contact metamorphosed by adjacent plutons 
into the amphibolite facies.
Sampling was intensive. The host rocks (HR) are represented by an 
average of 54 sites (-546 specimens) per deposit, and the BIF are 
represented by an average of 166 block samples (-895 specimens) per 
deposit. The quoted averages for the magnetic characteristics of each 
deposit therefore represent the value derived from several hundreds of 
measurements in each case.
MAGNETIC CHARACTERISTICS
The low field magnetic susceptibility values perpendicular to banding
-2 -3 for the BIF (k ) fall in a narrow range, and average 6.1 x 10 cgs cm
(Table 2). The values for HR (k. N have a much broader range reflecting. HR/
the variety of rock types sampled at each mine, however, because the ratio
of k T-7k TTn is ^00 in all four cases it is evident that the HR do not HR
contribute significantly to the measured magnetic anomaly over the BIF.
The average susceptibility of economic ore for the BIF deposits' is 10.5 i 3.6x10
-3(standard deviation) cgs cm . Also the average equation for relating

BIF has a very strong layer-controlled anisotropy of magnetic 
susceptibility CAMS) such that the susceptibility parallel to banding
(k,, .p-,) is about 1.62 times greater than that perpendicular to banding If JJ
(k -) , meaning that the measured magnetic response over the BIF is 
greatly enhanced relative to the expected value if the BIF is aligned 
nearly parallel to the Earth©s magnetic field CEMF) or greatly diminished 
if perpendicular to the EMF.
The measured natural remanent magnetization (NRM) for BIF (NRM.-) in
-2 these deposits fall within a consistent narrow range of 1.7 0.7 x 10
-3 emu cm . Their Koenigsberger ratio of remanent to induced magnetization
(QT-) also fall within a narrow-range of.0.61 0.10..©The values for the HR IF —A — ^ (NRM ) have an even broader range 6.4 ± 5.8 x 10 emu cm consistent
with the mixture of lithologies involved. Similarly Q has a broaderUK
range of 0.058 0.37. The important point coming out of these measurements 
is that the NRM is a significant contributor to the measured magneticl-c
anomaly whereas the NRM^ is so weak that it can be neglected. The net 
augmenting factor (NAF) is a measure of the increase in the measured 
field caused by the NRM component. For the four deposits NAF averages 
0.19 0.05 which means that the induced magnetization component of a 
BIF is increased by -19% by the addition of the NRM components.
MAGNETIC ANOMALY CALCULATION
The conventional interpretation of a magnetic anomaly utilizes the 
following parameters:

### page_18
1) a specific geometric model for the anomaly source. BIF deposits 
are chemical sediments which were originally deposited with long 
horizontal extents and relatively narrow thickness. Thus they are 
usually interpreted using a semi-infinite tabular sheet model using 
equations for a thin or thick sheet. We use the thick sheet model 
following equations from Telford et^ al^ (1976)}
2) the known average regional Earth©s magnetic field (EMF) values 
for its declination, inclination, and intensity at the BIF location;
3) magnetometer data including the measured component (i.e., the , 
total field, the vertical field, etc.), the terrain clearance of the 
magnetometer, and the residual anomaly characteristics (i.e., the 
difference between the measured magnetization of the anomaly and the 
Background magnetization if the anomaly were not present);
4) available geologic constraints which may be present for the BIF. 
These include: the length and strike direction which may be known from 
mapping but which also may be reliably estimated from the strike length 
magnetic profile and the elongation direction of the anomaly; the down-dip 
extent which is generally unknown; the d©ip angle which may or may not be 
known from mapping or drilling; the thickness of the BIF which may or 
may not be constrained by mapping or drilling; the low field magnetic 
susceptibility which may also be constrained if outcrop samples or core 
are available for measuring; and the thickness of overburden which may be 
zero if the BIF outcrops or may be known from drill data. Usually few, 
if any, of these constraints are known, so that the objective of analyzing 
the anomaly is to put realistic values on them. The most important
8

### page_19
parameters that are generally desired are estimates for the dip, thickness 
and percentage magnetite. With BIF of economic interest there are three 
factors which are generally not included in the calculation and thereby 
render a conventional interpretation meaningless. These are the AMS, 
the demagnetizing factor, and the NEM in order of relative importance.
Anisotropy of Magnetic Susceptibility
Noting that the average susceptibility for economic ore is .
-2 -3 k. - 10.5 x 10 cgs cm , and that k,. " 1.62 k, ,^,, the average bulk
magnetic susceptibility (BMS) for economic BIF ore of the four deposits
-2 -3 rs ~14.5 x 10 cgs cm . This average corresponds to the expected value
o
when the iron formation banding is intersected at an angle of ~32 to the EMF 
direction. The induced magnetization response is enhanced by +17% when 
the EMF is parallel to the banding and diminished by -25% when the EMF is 
perpendicular to the banding. Comparison of the anisotropy ratios
(k. T-i-./k. T ) for the four deposits with respect to metamorphic grade K . J-E j. JLt
reveals little difference. For example the average of the two ratio 
values for the less highly metamorphosed Sherman and Adams Mines is the 
same as the average for the two more highly metamorphosed Moose Mountain 
and Griffiths Mines, i.e., 1.63 to 1.61.
Demagnetizing Factor
The effect of the demagnetizing factor (DF) has been examined 
by Gay (1963). The value ranges from O for a long needle of 
susceptible material that is parallel to the EMF to Air for a 
needle perpendicular to the EMF. For a thick tabular sheet the 
value is 2ir provides a good estimate. Thus when BIF layers are

### page_20
parallel to the EMF, the DF has no effect; but when the EMF is 
perpendicular to the BIF layers, th.e measured response will be reduced 
to 68% of the expected "value.
Natural Remanent Magnetization
The NAF for the NRM of the four deposits is 0.19. or 19%. Given the 
large variety of attitudes of the BIF in these deposits, the NAF 
represents a reasonable value regardless of the attitude of a given BIF. 
The NAF represents the swing of viscous remanence components (VRM) into 
alignment with the EMF, and thus has the effect of increasing the induced 
magnetization regardless of the attitude of the BIF. The presence of 
significant VRM components is well documented from alternating field 
(AF) demagnetization, thermal (Th) demagnetization, and VRM decay tests 
such as storage and shock tests. The hard remanence components cannot 
be calculated in general terms unless the specific orientation of their 
vectors and their magnitudes are known.
Summary
Table 3 provides a general summary of the interaction for the AMS, 
DF, and NRM effects in BIF. The result is illustrated in Figure 1. 
Stated simply, the peak response of BIF that is parallel to the EMF in 
northern Ontario will be ~36% greater than expected using conventional 
anomaly interpretation formulas whereas if the BIF is perpendicular to 
the EMF it will be -30% smaller than expected.
The effect of© these factors on the shape of the anomaly is to 
remove virtually all dip-induced skew of the anomaly. Thus in northern

### page_23
Ontario, tlie shape of the measured anomaly will be nearly symmetrical. 
When the dip of the HIP is then calculated in a conventional way, it 
will be in the range of ~500N to vertical regardless of the true dip.
From the above discussion it is evident that exploration personnel 
looking for BIF in northern Ontario will typically choose only those 
anomalies for detailed work that are closely aligned to the EMF for 
which they will overestimate the "iron content thickness" product by 
~36%. Conversely anomalies caused by BIF oriented at a steep angle to 
the EMF will be interpreted as narrow or lean steeply-dipping BIF, and 
hence omitted from further exploration.
PALEOMAGNETIC RESULTS
Archean paleomagnetic remanence components were isolated in all 
four deposits both for the BIF and the HR. Some of the deposits 
retain minor post-Archean components associated with late basic dike 
intrusion, however, these are limited in sampling extent and are not 
considered here. The Archean pole positions are listed in Table 4 and 
illustrated in Figure 2 relative to the apparent polar wander path 
(APWP) for the Archean of North America CSeguin jrt al^ 1982). Two 
important points should be made. One is that fold and contact tests 
were used within each deposit to identify prefolding or postfolding 
Archean components. The second is that each BIF deposit has radically 
different strikes and dips, so that the agreement of the pole positions 
between deposits provides a very powerful fold test on a regional scale 
to further support the interpretation that the components are prefolding 
or postfolding in origin.

### page_26
The poorest agreement between the APWP and the determined pole 
positions is for the GMI component Ci. e., Griffith Mine //l). Several 
explanations are noted in the paper CSymons et^ al^ 1982) which focus on 
the fact that this deposit is in Uchi Belt rather than the Abitibi Belt 
from which the majority of the APWP data have been derived. TWO of the 
likelier explanations are the possibility that the B17 at the Griffith 
Mine is distinctly older than those of the Abitibi Belt so that its 
primary component predates the well defined portion of the Archean APWP, 
or alternatively that differential motions occurred between the Belts. 
Conversely the prefolding SM1, AMI and MM1 components from the Abitibi 
Belt form a well defined cluster at -2.75 Ga. These are considered to 
be primary depositional remanence components that have survived 
metamorphism.
Metamorphic or secondary remanence components that predate the 
Kenoran deformation include the SM2, MM2, and GM2. These form a. second 
group of poles at ~2.6 Ga and are thought to relate to the onset of the 
Kenoran orogeny. The GM3 component could also be considered in this 
group because it was acquired during deformation.
Only the AM2 component is considered to be a postfolding Kenoran 
orogenic overprint, and it was acquired at -2.45 Ga during cooling.
Similar components are likely present in the lower thermal and alternating-t
field coercivity spectra of the other deposits, however, they are hard to 
identify with certainty because they have the same direction as VT3M 
components associated with the EMF.

ABSTRACT
The -magnetic and paleomagnetic properties for the iron formation ClF) 
and host rocks CHR) are determined from a data base of -1600 specimens. 
The Algoman-type Banded iron formations have specific gravities (SG) 
ranging between 2.65 and 4.04 gem . The low-field susceptibility
perpendicular to banding (1O for IF has a lognormal mean of
 2 3 ~4.0 -x 10 cgs cm , so that k. ., ~ lllk.,-. The regression fit equation. ., J- J c
0.116 SG - 0.312 has a correlation coefficient of 40.85. The 
anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) of k M /kj^ relative to banding
is -1.52 for the IF. The mean natural remanent magnetization (NRM)
 2 5 -3 intensities for the IF and HR are 2.1 x 10 and 1.47 x 10 emu cm
which give mean Koenigsberger ratios of 0.66 and 0.051 respectively. 
Thus the HR contribution to the residual anomaly may be neglected. The 
NRM for the IF augments the calculated anomaly intensity by 14%. Combining 
the AMS and NRM augmenting effects with a demagnetizing factor of 2 77, 
yields theoretical anomaly calculations for the North and South Pit 
deposits that are within 10% of the measured anomalies in terms of peak 
intensity and half -width. Utilizing alternating field, thermal and 
chemical demagnetization techniques along with fold and contact tests for 
remanence stability leads to the isolation of three Archean remanence 
components in both the IF and HR. The GM2 component is the oldest at 
^2.8Ga and records primary deposition or diagenesis. It may also reflect 
tectonic motions between the Uchi and Abitibi Belts. The GM1 component 
is most prevalent and records a predeformational metamorphic event at 
~2.75 Ga. Its agreement with the primary components isolated in the
20

### page_31
Archean strata of the Abitibi Felt may indicate a genetic link between 
the two events. The GM3 component is dominantly but not entirely 
post-deformational, and appears to reflect Kenoran orogenic metamorphism 
at -2.6 Ga.

### page_32
INTRODUCTION
This study of the Algoman-type banded iron formation (IF) deposits 
at the Griffith Mine is- the final of four such studies. It follows the 
methods developed in three similar studies of the Sherman "Mine near 
Temagami CSymons and Stupavsky 1979, 1980), the Moose Mountain Mine near 
Capreol CSymons et al 1980), and the Adams Mine near Kirkland Lake (Symons 
et a^L 1980) in Ontario. The objects of these studies are to provide 
s-tatistically reliafile data for their magnetic properties so that the 
magnetic anomalies over IF may be correctly interpreted and to look at 
their paleomagnetic properties so that their ore genesis may be better 
understood.
The Griffith Mine is located -50 km south of Red Lake, Ontario 
C93022©W", 50048fN) along the west shore of Bruce Lake (Figure 1). 
Discovered prior to 1922 CBruce 19.24), the property was developed in the 
latter 1950*s and early 1960©s, and then brought into production by Steel 
Company of Canada and Pickards Mather and Company. It has a rated 
capacity of 1.4 x 10 tonnes of pellets per year.
GEOLOGY
The Griffiths IF deposit is located in the Uchi Belt of the Superior 
Province of The Canadian Shield. The oldest rocks are Archean metavolcanics 
comprised of tuff, agglomerate, rhyodacite and mafic members (Schelske 1970j 
Shklanka 1970)(Figure 2). Equivalent metavolcanics to the east give U-Pb 
zircon ages of 2959 ± 2 to 2738 ± 5 Ma (Nunes and Thurston 1980). Overlying 
the metavolcanics is a series of Archean metasediments of dominant greywacke 
composition which have been metamorphosed to quartz-plagioclase-biotite
22

### page_33
95
GRIFFITH 
MINE A.
Figure 1. Location of the Griffiths Mine

### page_35
schists with, accessory minerals including -magnetite, chlorite, sericite 
and epidote. The IF is interbedded with the metasediments. It is 
-80 m thick with, two members of magnetite-chert inter layered with 
recrystallized chert, three members of magnetite-rich biotite schistose 
IF, and a middle -20 m thick member of barren biotite schist and greywacke. 
Medium to high grade metamorphism is indicated by the presence of 
accessory amphibole, actinolite, garnet and andalusite. During the 
Kenoran orogeny at -2734 8 "Ma, the Archean strata was intensely deformed 
to produce tight isoclinal folds with related intense microfolding and 
foliations. This formed the North deposit as a syncline-anticline-syncline 
sequence which trends N300E and plunges at ~300SW and the South deposit 
as an overturned syncline-anticline which trends S270E and plunges at 
~600SE.
During the Kenoran orogeny-which peaked at -2734 8 Ma in the Uchi 
Belt, plutons were emplaced remote from the mine. Next hornblende-biotite 
diorite or quartz diorite plutons were emplaced which include the Bruce 
Pluton which forms the eastern wall rock for the deposits and extends 
nearly 60 km to the east, and the Pakwash Pluton which outcrops -2 km 
west of the deposits. These plutons are cut by several -50 cm wide 
feldspar porphyry, lamprophyre and gabbro dikes around Bruce Lake. The 
latter may be related to a large metagabbro pluton which is inferred from 
aeromagnetic data to underlie the northeastern part of the map area 
(ODM-GSC-1960). The latest intrusions in the area are muscovite-biotite 
granodiorite plutons with associated narrow aplite and pegmatite dikes 
found at the south end of Bruce Lake. Minor postemplacement shearing
25

### page_36
associated with late faults is found in these rocks and in the mafic 
dikes which, indicates a second minor period of deformation. Stockwell 
(1982) lists several K-Ar and Rb-Sr between -2700 and -2350 Ma for the 
plutonic rocks in the Uchi Belt which record various stages of epiKenoran 
cooling.
SAMPLING
At least 5 cores were drilled at each of 54 host rock (HR) sites from 
various units around the Griffith Mine area (Figure 2) which were oriented 
by solar compass. Two 2.50 cm diameter by 2.45 cm length specimens were 
sliced from each core giving 540 specimens. A total of 160 oriented hand 
samples of IF were collected from the North Pit and a further 15 from the 
South Pit (Figure 3). These were oriented by topographic sitings using 
bench mining maps. Four or more 0.95 cm right cylindrical specimens were 
cored from each hand sample giving a total 1070 IF specimens. Further 
explanation of the sampling , experimental methods and results of this 
study are given by Osmani (1982).

A modified picnometer method was used to measure the specific gravity
(SG), of 452 IF specimens (~3 per sample) to an accuracy of 0.001 g cm

relatively pure magnetite ore with a normal distribution having a mean of
3.36 0.31 (.standard deviation). Economic ore with an average of 317,
-3 total Fe has a SG of 3.60 g cm .

times on an aluminum plate with their NRM vector first parallel to the EMF 
and then again opposite to the EMF. This test resulted in an average
decrease in J of 44% combined with a NRM directional change of 290 . rl-F
Thus dynamite blasting in the deposits may have reduced the augmenting 
factor by as much as ~0.07 J., however, these VRM components are readily 
removed for paleomagnetic study by alternating field (AF) or thermal 
demagnetization.

MAGNETIC MODEL
The equations for a thick tabular sheet of infinite strike and dip 
extent are used to calculate the theoretical magnetic anomaly. Using 
the north limb of the North Pit as an example (Figure 11). The input 
data includes: 1} the EMF direction of 50 , 780 and intensity of
60,500 y (ODM-GSC 1960); 2) the IF strike of N300E, dip of 850E, and
-3 thickness of 60 m; 3) the IF k t susceptibility of 0.116 cgs cm and
k M /kj^ ratio of 1.52; 4) the demagnetizing factor of 27r; 5) the NRM 
augmenting factor of 0.14 J.; 6) the survey terrain clearance value of 
147 m. The calculated anomaly has a peak value of 9200y and a half- 
width of 177 m compared to the measured values of 9500Y and 145 m which 
represents a high degree of fit. For the South Pit equally good 
agreement was found with the calculated anomaly having a peak value of 
ll,414y and half -width of 169 m compared to the measured values of 
12, 500 Y and 161 m.

20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 80 and 100 mT peak fields. The paleomagnetic

to select the optimum cleaning field for the remaining specimens as 
well as vector removed data and stereocontour plots. Tectonic corrections 
include both plunge and tilt corrections.
Iron Formation
A representative selection of 58 pilot specimens of IF were tested. 
More than 90% of the specimens show a rapid decay of NKM intensity down 
to ^QZ of the original intensity by ~50 mT (Figure 12). Up to 20 mT
the specimens typically show rapid rates of directional motion of
deg T as VKM components are rapidly removed. Between ~20 and "40 mT,
the PSI are significantly *^100 deg T as characteristic directions are
isolated. Above "50 mT the acquisition of anhysteretic remanence (ARM) 
components produces PSI values of ^100 deg T~ . Accordingly the 
remaining specimens to give 4 per IF block sample were AF cleaned in 
fields of 30 or 40 mT. Conventional tiered statistics were first
attempted whereby specimens with anomalous directions ^20 0 from block
-7 -3 mean) , specimens with weak remanence ^5 x 10 emu cm ) , blocks with
"^2 reliable specimens, and block means with an ct^s^O0 were deemed 
unreliable. By this screening only 48 blocks, some with two component 
directions, or 27% of the collection yielded acceptable block mean 
directions. For collections of this type, modal or population level 
analysis (Symons and Stupavsky 1981; Van Alstine 1980) has proven more 
successful . In this method all vector directions for a single cleaning 
treatment are plotted on two stereonets C+ve inclinations on down

### page_53
hemisphere, -ve inclinations on up hemisphere) and contoured following 
the -method of Kamb (1959) with contour intervals in terms of standard 
deviations, i. e. , 2 is E H- 2cr or 2 standard deviations and therefore an 
anomaly outlined by the 2 contour has significance at >95% confidence, 
4 at >99.5% confidence, etc. The plots were run both with and without 
tectonic correction separating out the data for the east (El, E2, E3 
anomalies) and west (Wl, W2, W3 anomalies) limbs of the synclines 
forming the deposits and then combining the data. The results are shown 
in Figure 13 excluding the upper hemispheres which contain few data 
points. Fold tests indicate that the W3-E3 components combine to form 
the B component which is prefolding in origin with >>99% confidence, 
that the W2-E2 components combine to form the A component which is also 
prefolding in origin with >95% confidence, and that the W1-E1 components 
forming the C component are marginally postfolding in origin and appear 
to have been acquired when the folding was about 5C^ complete. The mean 
remanence directions and pole positions for A, B and C are given in 
Table 1.
HOST ROCK
One specimen per site or 54 HR specimens were AF step demagnetized. 
As expected they showed a wide range of NRM intensity decay patterns 
(Figure 14). On average they retained ~35% of their intensity at 50 mT 
and 20% at 100 mT. However, nearly all specimens showed small changes 
in NRM direction with PSI values of ^0 deg T" up to ~40 mT indicating 
quite stable remanence as their characteristic direction was isolated.

### page_58
Above -40 mT they showed an increasing scatter and correspondingly 
increasing PSI values as ARM components were added. Conventional 
tiered statistics after cleaning the remaining 8 specimens per site at 
their optimum field, mostly in the 20 to 40 mT range, led to the 
acceptance of only 19 site mean directions forming four directional 
clusters. Modal analysis defined these groupings far more clearly 
(Table 1). Fold tests on the D, E, and F components are equivocal.
THERMAL DEMAGNETIZATION 
IRON FORMATION
The 48 representative IF specimens behave quite similarly on thermal 
step demagnetization using steps of 100, 200, 300, 400, 450, 500, 550, 
575, 600, 625 and 6500C using a Schonstedt TSD1 oven. The intensity 
shows a rapid near linear drop to ~15% of the NRM intensity up to ~4000C, 
plateaus between 400 and 5000C, and then drops to ~IZ by 5500C (Figure 15) 
The remanence directions remain quite constant at a characteristic 
direction up to ~5000C and then scatter widely at higher temperatures. 
The isolated directions correspond mostly to the dominant W3-E3 components
with some residual W2-E2 components providing clear proof that these are 
the most stable components. A fold test on the combined population using 
the 450, 500 and 5500C directions proved inconclusive due to the scatter 
in directions caused by the mixture of components.
HOST ROCK
Similarly one HR specimen per site, or 54 in all, was thermally step 
demagnetized. Six specimens disintegrated by 6500C. Most specimens show

### page_60
a drop in NRM intensity up to ~2500C, a plateau at from 20 to 9C^ of 
their NRM intensity between ~2500C and ~5000C, and a rapid drop to "27* 
of their NRM intensity by ~5750C (Figure 16), thereby indicating the 
presence of considerable "single domain" magnetite as the stable 
remanence carrier. The directions show the isolation in the 500 to 5500C 
range of D, E but not F remanence components that are analogous to the 
A and B components isolated by AF cleaning. However 54 vector directions 
are insufficient for full modal analysis.
CONTACT TESTS
Two full and two partial contact tests were run on narrow (15 cm to 
l m wide) late basic dikes in contact with the HR. All tests were 
positive with the dike and baked zones (dike sites 7 and 32) or the dike 
only (dike sites 36 and 37) giving different remanence directions than 
the adjacent HR sites. The tests show that the remanence of the adjacent 
HR predates dike intrusion in the late Kenoran Orogeny.
POLE POSITIONS
The pole positions for the IF and HR components are given in Table l 
and shown in Figure 17 in relation to the apparent polar wander path of 
Seguin et al (1982) for the Archean time.
The IF B component is stable and definitely prefolding, and it 
(GM2 *) falls at ~2.7 Ga on the APW path. The HR E component is comparably 
stable and definitely predates dike intrusion, and it (GM2 A) similarly 
falls at "*2.7 Ga after tectonic correction. Thus both are regarded as 
equivalent predeformational Archean metamorphic components.

### page_62
KENORAN 
ARCHEAN
Figure 17. Apparent polar wander curve for the Archean of North America 
after Seguin ot^ al (1982) showing the pole positions for the 
IF and HR components listed in Table 1.
52

### page_63
The IF A component is also stable and prefolding in origin, however 
it (GM1 *) does not fall on any known segment of the Archean APW path. 
The HR D component is comparably stable and predates dike intrusion also. 
Its pole (GKL A) also falls off the APW path, and is the closest HR pole 
to GM1 A. The difference in the poles may reflect a real difference in 
time between deposition of the iron formation and the enclosing HR 
metavolcanic and metasedimentary strata. Several possible explanations 
are evident for the poles not falling on the APW path. One is that the 
path is defined primarily by units from the Abitibi belt so that pre 
2.7 Ga displacement between it and the Uchi belt is possible. Another 
is that the A and D components are not completely isolated so that a minor 
Kenoran orogeny component has biassed the poles to the north of the APW 
path. A third possibility is that the A and E components are -2.9 Ga in 
age and thus fall on an undefined segment of the APW path.
The IF C and HR F components are probably postfolding based on the 
IF fold test, however, tectonic correction has little effect on the 
locations of the pole positions in any event. Without correction both 
poles (GM3 *, GM3 A) fall beside on the APW path at -2.6 Ga which 
corresponds to the expected Kenoran Orogeny direction, and so both are 
interpreted to be Kenoran remagnetization overprints. This interpretation 
is supported by the fact that the HR sites contributing to this component 
come preferentially from the granodioritic Bruce Lake Pluton.
The dike poles are scattered with one close to the -2.6 Ga position 
on the APW path and three closer to the -1.7 Ga position (Irving 1979). 
This implies that the basic dikes may be very much younger than previously 
thought.
